Q: How to structure a Swift package(SPM)containing multiple packages(libraries/targets) and version them A:

You can't version individual targets/libraries independently within a single Package.swift. A Swift package is versioned as a whole via git tags on its repository, so newskit and the-sun in one manifest will always share the same version number, no matter how you split the targets.

There are a few real approaches depending on how independent you actually need the versioning to be:

1. Separate repositories per package (most common)

Split each library into its own git repo, each with its own Package.swift and its own tags. This is what most multi-package Swift projects do. Downside: you end up maintaining N repos instead of one, and cross-package changes need coordinated PRs across repos.

2. Git submodules / subtree

Keep one repo but pull each package in as a submodule (or split via git subtree) so each still resolves as its own git URL with its own tags. Works, but these workflows are notoriously fiddly to keep in sync.

3. A package registry (SE-0292)

Since SE-0292 added the package registry protocol, dependencies don't have to resolve via git URL at all. Once published to a registry, each package gets its own independent version (swift package-registry publish <scope>.<name> <version>), and publishing is per directory, so your monorepo's folder structure is entirely up to you. You can keep everything in one repo and still version newskit and the-sun completely independently.

Full disclosure, I built Perchly, a private registry that does exactly this, plus a small companion CLI (perchly-cli) that detects which package directories changed since the last publish and bumps/publishes just those. But this isn't registry-specific behavior, any SE-0292-compliant registry works the same way, it's what the protocol was designed for.

Q: Is it possible to reference an xml:id attribute in a CSS selector? A:

Intrinsic namespace defined for "xml:" prefix

You are missing the namespace in the CSS even though it's default in XML.

According this document:

https://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace

Quote:

The namespace whose name is http://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace is bound by definition to the prefix xml: according to Namespaces in XML (and by Namespaces in XML 1.1).

That means your xml: prefix intrinsically recognized by all XML renderers as the namespace http://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace . However, CSS does not know that. That's why when your original XML references the CSS without the namespace definition, it would not recognize it.

Add the namespace definition in CSS

The simplest solution is to add a namespace definition in CSS like so:

@namespace xml "http://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace";
foo[xml|id='bar']:after { content: " more stuff"; }

And then you can open a browser, such as FireFox, on the XML file:

<?xml-stylesheet href="foo.css"?>
<foo xml:id="bar">stuff</foo>

It should be correctly rendered as:

stuff more stuff

CSS qualified name

In CSS we need to use the vertical bar | to select the namespace, as explained in:

https://www.w3.org/TR/css-namespaces-3/

... in this section "4 CSS Qualified Names". Quote:

EXAMPLE 5

Given the namespace declarations:

   @namespace toto "http://toto.example.org";
   @namespace "http://example.com/foo";

In a context where the default namespace applies

toto|A

represents the name A in the http://toto.example.org namespace.

Q: xv6 add a system call that counts system calls A:

First comment:

You should place extern declarations in .h header files, which you include in both in the .c files that implements them and uses them. This will ensure that the datatype matches in both implementation and declaration.

The provides example code, and compiler output is far from complete, so hard to give exact problem. Possible causes:

  • you have other compiler warnings/errors too, like int16_t not declared, so the extern declaration was ignored.
  • the extern declaration was places too late in the file, after you wanted to use it.

Without complete code, this is a pure guessing game.
